The transition from perceived duration to the when of memory is likely shaped by attention and working memory (WM). In two experiments, we investigated how memory decay, interference between stored durations, and internal versus external attention affect the precision of recall from temporal WM. For this, we used a delayed reproduction task in which participants listened to a sequence of time intervals and reproduced them after a retention period (Herbst et al., 2025). In Experiment 1, we manipulated the ratio between the target interval and the retention interval, showing that both the duration of the retention interval (decay) and its ratio to the target (temporal distinctiveness yielding interference) affected WM performance. In Experiment 2, we examined interference between intervals within a sequence by manipulating attention via a cue indicating which interval to reproduce. The cue appeared either before (pro-cue) or after (retro-cue) the retention period, directing external attention to sensory encoding or internal attention to WM representations, respectively, either for a single item or the full sequence. External attention selectively benefited accuracy and precision for the longest item when cued alone in the final position. Retro-cueing, by contrast, more generally reduced precision for single-item compared to the whole-sequence recall. Finally, a mixture modeling approach revealed swap errors consistent with those observed in visual WM. Together, these findings compare the contributions of decay and temporal distinctiveness to temporal WM performance with a dynamic resource allocation faster thinkers are smarter thinkers: Working memory binding as the link between processing speed and cognitive ability","description":"Individuals who process information faster tend to score higher on cognitive ability tests, but the mechanism linking processing speed to general cognitive ability (g) remains unresolved. We tested whether this association is mediated by working memory capacity, and if so, whether the critical component is executive attention — as captured by complex span tasks requiring dual-task coordination and interference management — or relational binding — the ability to form and maintain temporary associations between unrelated features. In a community sample of 215 adults (aged 18–40), we measured processing speed at both the neural level (ERP component peak latencies) and the cognitive level (diffusion model drift rates), working memory through complex span and binding tasks, and g through a comprehensive cognitive ability test battery. Latent variable mediation analyses showed that complex span performance only partially mediated the speed–g relationship, leaving significant direct effects. In contrast, binding task performance fully mediated the relationship for cognitive processing speed and substantially mediated it for neural processing speed, reducing previously significant direct paths to nonsignificance. When both mediators competed in parallel models, binding emerged as the dominant predictor of g, with complex span contributing no unique variance. These findings identify relational binding as the specific working memory component that transmits the association between processing speed and cognitive ability, suggesting that the cognitive bottleneck linking processing speed to reasoning ability is not executive control but the more elemental ability to build and maintain temporary relational A test of episodic memory with a shelf task","description":"Immersive virtual reality (IVR) has been proposed as a bridge between laboratory studies and real-world behavior, offering both high experimental control and ecological validity. However, studies directly comparing virtual and real-world replicas remain scarce. The present study investigated three experimental conditions—IVR, non-immersive VR (N-IVR), and Reality—focusing on subjective experiences and episodic memory performance. Participants (N = 156) were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions and completed a Shelf Task involving two encoding sessions in which they placed 8 objects on a shelf per session, followed by two recall sessions 10 minutes later. After encoding, participants rated subjective experiences, including spatial presence (self-location and action possibilities), similarity to daily life, enjoyment, cybersickness, and game mechanics. Overall, IVR approximated real-world experience more closely than N-IVR. Ratings of action possibilities and similarity to daily life in IVR matched Reality, and IVR elicited higher enjoyment than both N-IVR and Reality. Some differences remained: self-location and game mechanics favored Reality, and cybersickness was unique to IVR, though at low levels. Memory performance revealed robust session × condition effects. In Session 1, IVR recall lagged behind N-IVR and Reality, suggesting initial challenges with IVR encoding. By Session 2, IVR performance improved markedly, reaching levels comparable to N-IVR for free recall and to both Reality and N-IVR for spatial recall. These findings highlight both the promise and limitations of IVR: it can closely approximate real-world experience and memory performance over repeated exposure, but subjective and embodied aspects of reality are not fully replicated. The results have implications for experimental and applied cognitive assessment, as well as clinical and training
